claims.text: Hydrogen spillover-driven synthesis can stabilize high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed stabilization remains effective during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
The starting nanoparticles contain five or more metals in a near-equiatomic composition.
The starting nanoparticles are crystalline solid solutions.
Hydrogen spillover can be used to synthesize high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Hydrogen spillover is energetically favored on reducible oxide surfaces.
The intervention produces a single-phase FCC structure.
Hydrogen spillover causes simultaneous reduction of all constituent metal ions.
Simultaneous reduction of all metal ions produces a stable multielement solid solution.
The treated nanoparticles will be more stable than untreated nanoparticles.
The treated nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than untreated nanoparticles.
The intervention is applicable generally to near-equiatomic compositions containing five or more metals.
The resulting nanoparticles are suitable for high-temperature catalytic applications.

contradictions.description: The intervention is framed as being applied to already crystalline solid-solution nanoparticles, whereas the stated mechanism is precursor-ion reduction during nanoparticle synthesis.
The mechanism is stated definitively as simultaneous reduction of all metal ions, while the uncertainty field says that the exact mechanism is uncertain.
The predicted-outcome baseline is 'untreated nanoparticles,' but the proposed experiment uses nanoparticles made by traditional synthesis methods; these are not necessarily the same control.
